explanations.explanation: Right on the money, baker. Paul doesn't point at the weather or the headlines. He points at people, and then the list rolls in: "lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant…" (2 Timothy 3:2). I think that's Paul saying the trouble starts in the heart. Notice he puts the whole mess on what people are like, and that's where he keeps his eyes.

Wars sound like a safe guess, and I get it. But Paul never mentions a single battle here. He says "men will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant…" (2 Timothy 3:2). The terrible part is how people will be, not what armies are doing. Paul puts his finger on people and keeps it there.

Empty pantries make for a rough time, no doubt. But Paul doesn't say a word about hunger in this passage. He says "men will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant…" (2 Timothy 3:2). The terrible times he describes come from what people are like, not from what's missing off the shelf.

That's the one, baker. Paul says it short and sharp: "Turn away from such as these!" (2 Timothy 3:5). No long meeting, no group chat about it. When a box is all bow and no cookies, you set it down and walk away. Paul gives Timothy a clear instruction and doesn't dress it up.

Whoa, hold the oven door on that one! Paul says the opposite. He tells Timothy, "Turn away from such as these!" (2 Timothy 3:5). Paul doesn't hand these people a classroom. They have a form of godliness but deny its power, so Timothy is told to walk away from them.

I can see the appeal, baker. A big showdown with folding chairs and a microphone. But that's not what Paul writes. He says, "Turn away from such as these!" (2 Timothy 3:5). That's a turn, not a debate. Paul's instruction here is to walk the other way.

explanations.answer: They never come to know the truth
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! Paul says they are "always learning but never able to come to a knowledge of the truth." (2 Timothy 3:7). That's a baker who reads every recipe in the world and never once turns on the oven. All that learning, and the truth never lands. Paul names that gap and doesn't soften it.

explanations.answer: They never share what they learn
explanations.explanation: Good thinking, but Paul never says a word about sharing. He says these women are "always learning but never able to come to a knowledge of the truth." (2 Timothy 3:7). The catch isn't what they do with their learning. It's that they never arrive at the truth. Always learning, never landing.

Close to the neighborhood, but not the house. Paul doesn't say anything about trust here. He says they are "always learning but never able to come to a knowledge of the truth." (2 Timothy 3:7). The catch is that the learning never gets them to the truth. And honestly, I think a lot of us know what it's like to keep learning and keep circling.

That's it, baker. Paul says these men "are depraved in mind and disqualified from the faith." (2 Timothy 3:8). It's a heavy word, and he means it. Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, and Paul says these men oppose the truth in the same way. Paul keeps it plain.

Oh, I wish I could give you that one, baker. Paul says nothing about brilliance. He says they are "depraved in mind and disqualified from the faith." (2 Timothy 3:8). Their minds are described as depraved, not brilliant. A fancy hat on a cookie box doesn't change what's inside.

Curious sounds so harmless, doesn't it? But that's not Paul's word. He says these men "are depraved in mind and disqualified from the faith." (2 Timothy 3:8). The word he picks is depraved. They oppose the truth, just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, Israel's leader.

You got it, baker. Paul says these men "are depraved in mind and disqualified from the faith." (2 Timothy 3:8). He says it right after saying they oppose the truth. It's a serious line, and Paul states it plainly. I think that's why he told Timothy to turn away from them (2 Timothy 3:5).

Not this time, baker. Paul does say it, and he says it straight: these men are "depraved in mind and disqualified from the faith." (2 Timothy 3:8). The words are right there in the verse. It's a heavy line, and the answer is True.

I can see why that one tempts you, baker. But Paul says the opposite: "But they will not advance much further." (2 Timothy 3:9). These men have a limit. They're not climbing forever. Paul says it right there in the verse, and the answer is False.

Yes, baker, and what a relief! Paul says, "But they will not advance much further." (2 Timothy 3:9). After that long list, he lets Timothy know it won't go on forever. These men run out of road. That's good news after all those terrible times.

Baked right, baker! Paul says "their folly will be plain to everyone." (2 Timothy 3:9). Paul says it will be out in the open, just like it was with Jannes and Jambres. No hiding it behind a pretty bow. That's the kind of ending that makes me smile.

That one has it backward, baker. Paul says "their folly will be plain to everyone." (2 Timothy 3:9). Nothing stays unknown here. It will be out where everybody can see it, just like with Jannes and Jambres. The word is plain.

Pleasing? Oh, friend, I wish. But Paul says "their folly will be plain to everyone." (2 Timothy 3:9). Folly isn't something anyone ends up enjoying. Paul says it will be plain for all to see, just like Jannes and Jambres.
